Method A.summary: Survey the polling place whose previous-election result was closest to the district total.

Method B.summary: Stratify stations by previous-election results and sample stations from every stratum.

Method C.summary: Visit all polling stations in turn and survey for a set time at each.

c1.text: Method A compares each polling station's result in the previous election with the overall district tally and surveys the station where the difference is smallest.

c2.text: Voting behavior at each polling station is similar to that in the previous election.

c3.text: Method A yields a representative sample of the district.

c4.text: Method B groups polling stations with similar party-specific results in the previous election into strata and randomly selects stations from each stratum in proportion to voters.

c5.text: Polling stations within the same district are heterogeneous in voters' political orientation.

c6.text: Polling stations within the same district are generally homogeneous in voters' political orientation.

c7.text: Method B yields a representative sample of the district.

c8.text: Method C travels to all polling stations in the district, surveying at each for a set time, with sample sizes proportional to the number of eligible voters.

c9.text: Method C does not need previous-election vote counts per polling station.

c10.text: Method C yields a representative sample of the district.

c11.text: In method C, data from the previous election about vote counts per polling station is essential.

h1.text: The population's social characteristics at a polling station have changed significantly since the last election.

h2.text: Voting behavior at that polling station may differ considerably from the previous election.

a.note: 'Difficult to apply' read as: the change undermines A's assumption c2, so A's representativeness is weakened.

b.note: B assumes heterogeneity (c5), the contrary of c6.

c.note: C derives c9 (data not needed), the contrary of c11.
